title: Prospective Drug Utilization Review and the Patient Profile It Runs On
topic: Patient care / Prospective drug utilization review and the patient profile
subtopic: The statutory prospective drug review in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A, the drug utilization review required by 247 CMR 9.17(1), the responsive-measure and documentation duties in 247 CMR 9.17(2), the current-standards requirement in 247 CMR 9.17(3), and the confidential patient profile, immediate-retrieval and reasonable-effort duties in 247 CMR 9.16(7) and 9.16(8)
learning_objectives: State the trigger for the prospective drug review in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A and the trigger for the drug utilization review in 247 CMR 9.17(1), and say precisely where the two differ.
Explain why the screening and identification lists attached to both mandates are permissive while the duty to conduct the review is not.
Set out what 247 CMR 9.16(7) requires a confidential patient profile to contain, and identify which of its duties is qualified by reasonable effort and which is not.
Apply the immediate-retrieval requirement to a pharmacy whose system cannot show previously dispensed drugs when the prescription is presented.
State the standard a drug utilization review must rest on under 247 CMR 9.17(3), and explain why a named work in a superseded edition can fail it while an unnamed current source can satisfy it.
Separate the discretionary choice of responsive measure in 247 CMR 9.17(2) from the mandatory record of whatever measure was taken.
Apply the inpatient carve-out in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A to a particular dispensing, and state what the carve-out attaches to.
Identify the exclusion in 247 CMR 9.16(8) and name the pharmacies it removes from 247 CMR 9.16.

orientation.text: Massachusetts imposes the prospective review twice, once by statute and once by regulation, and the two versions do not say quite the same thing. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A opens by providing that a pharmacist shall conduct a prospective drug review before each new prescription is dispensed or delivered to a patient or a person acting on behalf of such patient. 247 CMR 9.17(1) provides that a pharmacist shall conduct a prospective drug utilization review, which the regulation abbreviates to DUR, before each new prescription or medication order is dispensed or delivered to a patient or a patient's agent. Both fix the moment of the duty at dispensing or delivery rather than at the moment the prescription arrives, and both reach a handover made to somebody other than the patient. The regulation is the wider of the two on its face, because it adds the medication order to the prescription. Neither provision makes the duty turn on how the prescription reached the pharmacy, and neither waits for the patient to ask.

What follows each mandate is a list, and in both places the list is the permissive half of the provision. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A the review may include, but not be limited to, screening for potential drug therapy problems due to therapeutic duplication, drug disease contraindication, drug interactions including serious interactions with nonprescription or over-the-counter drugs, incorrect drug dosage, duration of drug treatment, drug allergy interactions and clinical abuse or misuse. Under 247 CMR 9.17(1) the DUR may include a review of computerized alerts, the patient record, and each new and renewed prescription or medication order for the purpose of promoting therapeutic appropriateness, by making a reasonable effort to identify over-utilization or under-utilization, therapeutic duplication, drug-disease contraindication, drug-drug interaction, drug-food interaction, incorrect drug dosage or duration of drug treatment, drug-allergy interactions, abuse or misuse, any significant change in drug, dose, or directions, and any age related contraindications. The verb governing each list is may, while the verb governing the review itself is shall. Reading the list as the definition of the duty inverts the provision, and a pharmacist who has ticked every named item has not thereby answered the question the provision actually asks.

The review is not conducted on the prescription alone. 247 CMR 9.16(7) requires a pharmacist and pharmacy to maintain a confidential patient profile for each patient to whom a prescription is dispensed, and 247 CMR 9.17(1) names the patient record among the material a DUR may review. The profile is therefore the standing record the review runs on, and it is built before the individual dispensing rather than assembled at the counter. The pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee shall make a reasonable effort to obtain, record, and maintain the name, address, contact information, date of birth or age, and gender of the patient for whom the prescription is intended; the patient history, including known drug allergies and drug reactions; a comprehensive list of medications and relevant devices dispensed by the pharmacy; and the pharmacist's comments relevant to the patient's drug therapy.

Within that one paragraph sit two duties of different character, and the examinable point is that the qualifier on the first does not travel to the second. The content duty is qualified: the standard is a reasonable effort to obtain, record, and maintain, so an incomplete profile is not automatically a breach, and a pharmacy that simply never asked is not saved by the fact that the standard is effort rather than result. What is being graded is what the pharmacy did. The system duty carries no such qualifier. 247 CMR 9.16(7) provides flatly that the computerized pharmacy system shall provide for the immediate retrieval of information necessary for the pharmacist to identify previously dispensed drugs at the time the prescription is presented for dispensing. A system that surfaces that information only after an overnight batch, or only on a call to another office, does not meet it, and diligent questioning at the counter is not offered by the regulation as a substitute. 247 CMR 9.16(8) then removes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from the requirements in 247 CMR 9.16 altogether.

A review has to be measured against something, and 247 CMR 9.17(3) supplies the standard: the DUR shall be based upon current standards which may include the American Hospital Formulary Service Drug Information, the United States Pharmacopoeia Drug Information, the American Medical Association Drug Evaluations, Plumb's Veterinary Drug Handbook, and other peer-reviewed medical literature. Two features of that sentence do the work. The operative requirement is currency, carried by the word shall, so a source that is out of date fails whatever its title; and the list is open, both because it is introduced by may include and because its final item is a category rather than a work. A superseded edition of a named compendium is therefore not rescued by the fact that the compendium is named, and a current peer-reviewed source is not disqualified by the fact that it is not.

Finding something is not the end of the pharmacist's obligation. 247 CMR 9.17(2) provides that upon identifying any of the above, meaning any of the items the preceding paragraph lists, a pharmacist shall take appropriate measures to ensure the proper care of the patient, which may include consultation with the prescribing practitioner or direct consultation with the patient or patient's agent. The choice among measures belongs to the pharmacist, and the two named consultations are examples rather than a required sequence. The sentence that follows is not permissive at all: a pharmacist shall document any measures taken in response to a drug utilization review. That record duty stands on its own. It is owed on the measure taken rather than on the seriousness of the finding, and it is not discharged by resolving the clinical problem before anything is dispensed. Direct consultation with the patient under 247 CMR 9.17(2) is a response to a review finding, and it should not be confused with the separate offer-to-counsel regime, which other provisions carry and which this section does not treat.

One limit sits on the statutory duty and has to be placed accurately. The final paragraph of M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A provides that the provisions of that section shall not apply to any drug dispensed to an inpatient at a hospital or nursing home, except to the extent required by regulations promulgated by the Federal Health Care Financing Administration pursuant to 42 USC 1396r-8. Two things follow from the way it is worded. The carve-out attaches to the drug dispensed and to the patient's inpatient status, not to the pharmacy, its licence or its address, so a hospital pharmacy that also dispenses at an outpatient window is outside the carve-out for the outpatient dispensings it makes. And the carve-out names nursing homes alongside hospitals, so a candidate who remembers only the hospital half will misplace a nursing-home inpatient. The carve-out is stated in the statute, and it is not repeated in the text of 247 CMR 9.17.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacist reviewing a new prescription for an 84-year-old patient sees an age related contraindication among the computerized alerts. She speaks directly to the patient's daughter, who is collecting the prescription on the patient's behalf, explains the risk and what to watch for, and dispenses the prescription unchanged. She records nothing, on the footing that no therapy changed and that the alert is already stored in the dispensing system. What is still owed?
steps: Confirm the review was owed at all. 247 CMR 9.17(1) fixes the duty before each new prescription or medication order is dispensed or delivered to a patient or a patient's agent, and a daughter collecting on the patient's behalf is within that.

Place the finding on the list. Any age related contraindications is the last of the items 247 CMR 9.17(1) sets out, so what she identified is one of the above for the purposes of the paragraph that follows.

Read the response duty. 247 CMR 9.17(2) required appropriate measures to ensure the proper care of the patient, and direct consultation with the patient's agent is one of the two measures that paragraph names, so speaking to the daughter was a permitted measure.

Read the sentence after it. A pharmacist shall document any measures taken in response to a drug utilization review. That sentence is not conditioned on the therapy changing, on the seriousness of the finding, or on the outcome.

Separate the alert from the record. 247 CMR 9.17(1) treats computerized alerts as material a DUR may review, so the stored alert evidences an input to the review rather than the measure taken in response to it.
worked_examples.resolution: The consultation was a proper measure, but the record of it is still owed under 247 CMR 9.17(2). The error the scenario invites is treating a resolved clinical problem as a closed file, and then offering the system's own alert log as the record; what the regulation asks for is a record of the measure the pharmacist took, and the alert is an input to the review rather than a response to it.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy keeps meticulous profiles. Every patient is asked about allergies and current medicines, the answers are recorded, and the pharmacist's comments are kept up to date. Its dispensing system, however, holds previously dispensed drugs on a central server that the branch can query only by telephoning head office in business hours, so at the counter the pharmacist cannot see what the pharmacy dispensed last month. The manager says the profile duty is a reasonable-effort duty and the pharmacy plainly meets it. Is that right?
steps: Split 247 CMR 9.16(7) into its two duties before judging anything, because the paragraph states a content duty and a system duty in successive sentences.

Test the content duty on its own standard. The pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee shall make a reasonable effort to obtain, record, and maintain the listed information, and on these facts that effort is being made.

Test the system duty on its own words. The computerized pharmacy system shall provide for the immediate retrieval of information necessary for the pharmacist to identify previously dispensed drugs at the time the prescription is presented for dispensing, and nothing in that sentence is qualified by effort.
Apply that to the facts. A query that depends on a telephone call to head office in business hours is not immediate retrieval at the time the prescription is presented.
Check the exclusion before finishing. 247 CMR 9.16(8) removes the requirements in 247 CMR 9.16 from institutional sterile compounding pharmacies, and this pharmacy is not one of those.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacy satisfies the content duty and fails the system duty. The error the scenario invites is carrying the reasonable-effort standard across the whole of 247 CMR 9.16(7), so that thorough questioning at the counter is put forward in place of a system that can retrieve previously dispensed drugs when the prescription is presented.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacist conducting a drug utilization review wants a dosing reference for a veterinary patient and reaches for Plumb's Veterinary Drug Handbook. A colleague objects that the regulation is concerned with human drug information and tells her to rely instead on the pharmacy's shelf copy of a named human compendium, an edition superseded in 2014, because that work is named in the regulation. Which source may the review rest on?
steps: Read 247 CMR 9.17(3) as a whole. The DUR shall be based upon current standards which may include the five items the paragraph then lists.
Note what is actually named. Plumb's Veterinary Drug Handbook is item (d) of that list, so the colleague's premise that the named works are all human compendia is wrong on the face of the regulation.
Identify the operative requirement. The mandatory word attaches to current standards, and naming a work does nothing to make a superseded edition of it current.
Apply the open end of the list. Item (e) is other peer-reviewed medical literature, so a current source the paragraph does not name is not excluded for want of a mention.
worked_examples.resolution: She may found the review on the current Plumb's Veterinary Drug Handbook and may not found it on the 2014 edition of the named human compendium. The error the scenario invites is reading a named list in a regulation as a closed list of permitted sources, and then treating the title of the work rather than the currency of the edition as the thing 247 CMR 9.17(3) actually requires.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy serves a hospital campus. It dispenses to inpatients on the wards, to residents of an attached nursing home, and to members of the public at a window in the lobby. Its director proposes one policy: because the statutory prospective drug review does not apply to inpatients, the pharmacy will treat the statutory duty as inapplicable to everything it dispenses on the campus, and will treat nursing-home residents as covered by the statute because a nursing home is not a hospital. Where does that go wrong?
steps: Read the carve-out where it sits. The final paragraph of M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A provides that the provisions of the section shall not apply to any drug dispensed to an inpatient at a hospital or nursing home.
Notice what the carve-out attaches to. It attaches to the drug dispensed and to the patient's inpatient status, not to the pharmacy, its licence or its address.
Apply it to the lobby window. A member of the public collecting a new prescription there is not an inpatient, so the statutory review under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A is owed for that dispensing.
Apply it to the nursing home. The carve-out names an inpatient at a hospital or nursing home, so a nursing-home inpatient falls inside the carve-out rather than outside it.
Keep the federal reservation in view. The carve-out itself yields to the extent required by regulations promulgated by the Federal Health Care Financing Administration pursuant to 42 USC 1396r-8.
worked_examples.resolution: Both halves of the proposed policy are wrong, and in opposite directions. The error the scenario invites is turning a carve-out that operates dispensing by dispensing into a status the whole pharmacy enjoys, while dropping the nursing home out of a carve-out that names it.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The statutory prospective drug review is owed before each new prescription is ______ or ______ to a patient or ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: dispensed; delivered; a person acting on behalf of such patient, under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does 247 CMR 9.17(1) add to the trigger that the statute does not carry?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The medication order. The regulation requires the DUR before each new prescription or medication order is dispensed or delivered to a patient or a patient's agent.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a pharmacist who has checked every screening item the statute names has by that fact discharged the statutory review.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A provides that the review may include, but not be limited to, those items. The list is permissive; the review is compulsory.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which two duties does 247 CMR 9.16(7) state, and which of them is qualified by reasonable effort?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The content duty to obtain, record and maintain the profile information, which is qualified by reasonable effort, and the system duty of immediate retrieval, which is not qualified at all.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: By when must the computerized pharmacy system be able to identify previously dispensed drugs?
retrieval_prompts.answer: At the time the prescription is presented for dispensing, under 247 CMR 9.16(7).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the four categories of information 247 CMR 9.16(7) requires a reasonable effort to obtain, record and maintain.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The name, address, contact information, date of birth or age, and gender of the patient for whom the prescription is intended; the patient history, including known drug allergies and drug reactions; a comprehensive list of medications and relevant devices dispensed by the pharmacy; and the pharmacist's comments relevant to the patient's drug therapy.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which pharmacies does 247 CMR 9.16(8) remove from the requirements in 247 CMR 9.16?
A drug utilization review shall be based upon ______ standards, and the fifth item on the list is ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: current; other peer-reviewed medical literature, under 247 CMR 9.17(3), which is what keeps the list open.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 9.17(2), which part of the pharmacist's response is discretionary and which is mandatory?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The choice of measure is discretionary, because consultation with the prescribing practitioner and direct consultation with the patient or patient's agent are given as examples. Documenting any measures taken is mandatory.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does resolving the clinical problem before dispensing discharge the record duty in 247 CMR 9.17(2)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. A pharmacist shall document any measures taken in response to a drug utilization review, and that duty is not conditioned on the outcome.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: To what does the inpatient carve-out in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A attach, and what does it yield to?
retrieval_prompts.answer: To any drug dispensed to an inpatient at a hospital or nursing home, so it operates dispensing by dispensing rather than pharmacy by pharmacy, and it yields to the extent regulations under 42 USC 1396r-8 require.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Is a stored computerized alert the record that 247 CMR 9.17(2) requires?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. 247 CMR 9.17(1) treats computerized alerts as material a DUR may review, so an alert is an input; 247 CMR 9.17(2) requires a record of the measures the pharmacist took in response.

quick_review.text: A pharmacist shall conduct a prospective drug review before each new prescription is dispensed or delivered to a patient or a person acting on behalf of such patient, under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A.

The statutory screening list is introduced by may include, but not be limited to, and covers potential drug therapy problems due to therapeutic duplication, drug disease contraindication, drug interactions including serious interactions with nonprescription or over-the-counter drugs, incorrect drug dosage, duration of drug treatment, drug allergy interactions and clinical abuse or misuse.

247 CMR 9.17(1) requires the prospective drug utilization review before each new prescription or medication order is dispensed or delivered to a patient or a patient's agent, so the regulatory trigger is wider than the statutory one.

The ten items in 247 CMR 9.17(1) run from over-utilization or under-utilization through drug-food interaction and any significant change in drug, dose, or directions to any age related contraindications, and they sit in the sentence that says the DUR may include a reasonable effort to identify them.
A pharmacist and pharmacy shall maintain a confidential patient profile for each patient to whom a prescription is dispensed, under 247 CMR 9.16(7).

The computerized pharmacy system shall provide for the immediate retrieval of information necessary for the pharmacist to identify previously dispensed drugs at the time the prescription is presented for dispensing, and that requirement is not qualified by effort.

The profile content duty in 247 CMR 9.16(7) is a reasonable effort to obtain, record, and maintain patient identifiers, patient history including known drug allergies and drug reactions, a comprehensive list of medications and relevant devices dispensed by the pharmacy, and the pharmacist's comments relevant to the patient's drug therapy.
247 CMR 9.16(8) provides that the requirements in 247 CMR 9.16 do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

The DUR shall be based upon current standards which may include the American Hospital Formulary Service Drug Information, the United States Pharmacopoeia Drug Information, the American Medical Association Drug Evaluations, Plumb's Veterinary Drug Handbook, and other peer-reviewed medical literature, under 247 CMR 9.17(3).

Currency is the governing requirement in 247 CMR 9.17(3): a superseded edition of a named work fails it, and a current source the paragraph does not name can satisfy it as other peer-reviewed medical literature.

On identifying any of the items listed in 247 CMR 9.17(1), a pharmacist shall take appropriate measures to ensure the proper care of the patient, which may include consultation with the prescribing practitioner or direct consultation with the patient or patient's agent.
A pharmacist shall document any measures taken in response to a drug utilization review, and that duty in 247 CMR 9.17(2) survives the resolution of the clinical problem.

decision_logic.condition: A new prescription is about to be dispensed or delivered.
decision_logic.action: Conduct the prospective review before the handover, not after it. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A fixes the duty before the prescription is dispensed or delivered, and 247 CMR 9.17(1) fixes it before each new prescription or medication order is dispensed or delivered.

decision_logic.condition: Someone other than the patient is collecting, or delivery is being made to someone else.
decision_logic.action: Run the review anyway. The statute reaches a person acting on behalf of such patient and 247 CMR 9.17(1) reaches a patient's agent, so the identity of the person at the counter does not switch the duty off.

decision_logic.condition: A candidate is asked whether checking the listed screening items completes the review.
decision_logic.action: Read the introductory words before the list. In both M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A and 247 CMR 9.17(1) the list is permissive and the review is mandatory, so completing the list is not the test.

Ask what the pharmacy did rather than what the record shows. 247 CMR 9.16(7) sets a reasonable effort to obtain, record, and maintain, so a refusal after being asked is tolerated and a failure to ask is not.

decision_logic.condition: The dispensing system cannot show previously dispensed drugs at the counter.
decision_logic.action: Do not import the reasonable-effort standard. 247 CMR 9.16(7) requires the computerized pharmacy system to provide for immediate retrieval at the time the prescription is presented for dispensing, and the shortfall is in the system rather than in the effort.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacy is an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Apply 247 CMR 9.16(8) first: the requirements in 247 CMR 9.16 do not reach it, so the profile and retrieval analysis stops before it begins.

decision_logic.condition: A source is offered as the basis for a drug utilization review.
decision_logic.action: Test currency before pedigree. 247 CMR 9.17(3) requires current standards, and the five items it lists are introduced by may include, so an unnamed current source is admissible and a superseded edition of a named one is not.

Choose a measure appropriate to the proper care of the patient, using consultation with the prescribing practitioner or direct consultation with the patient or patient's agent if either fits, and then document the measure taken, because 247 CMR 9.17(2) makes the record duty unconditional.

decision_logic.condition: A dispensing is said to fall outside the statutory review.
decision_logic.action: Ask whether this drug is being dispensed to an inpatient at a hospital or nursing home. The carve-out in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A runs on the dispensing and the patient's status, and it yields to the extent regulations under 42 USC 1396r-8 require.

ma_vs_federal.text: The inpatient carve-out in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A is not absolute against federal law: the section does not apply to a drug dispensed to an inpatient at a hospital or nursing home except to the extent required by regulations promulgated by the Federal Health Care Financing Administration pursuant to 42 USC 1396r-8, so a federal requirement can pull an inpatient dispensing back into the duty.

exceptions.text: M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A does not apply to any drug dispensed to an inpatient at a hospital or nursing home, except to the extent required by regulations promulgated under 42 USC 1396r-8. The carve-out attaches to the dispensing and the patient's status, so an outpatient dispensing by the same pharmacy stays inside the section.

247 CMR 9.16(8) provides that the requirements in 247 CMR 9.16 do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies, which removes both the profile content duty and the immediate-retrieval duty from those pharmacies.

timing_deadlines.event: Statutory prospective drug review of a new prescription
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Before the prescription is dispensed or delivered to the patient or a person acting on behalf of the patient
timing_deadlines.consequence: The review must be complete before the handover; a review conducted afterwards is not the review M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A requires.

timing_deadlines.event: Regulatory drug utilization review of a new prescription or medication order
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Before the prescription or medication order is dispensed or delivered to a patient or a patient's agent
timing_deadlines.consequence: The duty under 247 CMR 9.17(1) attaches to each new prescription and to each new medication order, so a medication order that is dispensed without a DUR is not covered by having reviewed the prescriptions alongside it.

timing_deadlines.event: Retrieval of previously dispensed drugs from the computerized pharmacy system
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Immediately, at the time the prescription is presented for dispensing
timing_deadlines.consequence: A system that produces the information only later, however reliably, does not meet 247 CMR 9.16(7), and no amount of questioning at the counter substitutes for it.

timing_deadlines.event: Documenting the measures taken in response to a drug utilization review
timing_deadlines.timeframe: 247 CMR 9.17(2) fixes no period; the duty attaches to the measure itself
timing_deadlines.consequence: The record is owed whenever a measure is taken, and it is owed whether or not the clinical problem was resolved before dispensing.

forms_records.text: The confidential patient profile required by 247 CMR 9.16(7) records the name, address, contact information, date of birth or age, and gender of the patient for whom the prescription is intended; the patient history, including known drug allergies and drug reactions; a comprehensive list of medications and relevant devices dispensed by the pharmacy; and the pharmacist's comments relevant to the patient's drug therapy.

247 CMR 9.17(2) requires a record of the measures taken in response to a drug utilization review. What is recorded is the measure, so a note that an alert fired says nothing about what the pharmacist did about it.

A computerized alert is an input rather than a record of the response: 247 CMR 9.17(1) lists a review of computerized alerts among the things the DUR may include, while the record duty sits in 247 CMR 9.17(2).

role_duties.duty: Conduct the prospective drug review before each new prescription is dispensed or delivered under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A, and the prospective drug utilization review before each new prescription or medication order is dispensed or delivered under 247 CMR 9.17(1).

role_duties.role: Pharmacist responding to a review finding
role_duties.duty: Take appropriate measures to ensure the proper care of the patient, choosing among measures such as consultation with the prescribing practitioner or direct consultation with the patient or patient's agent, and document any measures taken.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist choosing the basis for a review
role_duties.duty: Rest the drug utilization review on current standards, which may include the four works named in 247 CMR 9.17(3) and other peer-reviewed medical literature.
Make a reasonable effort to obtain, record, and maintain the patient profile information listed in 247 CMR 9.16(7).

Maintain a confidential patient profile for each patient to whom a prescription is dispensed, and keep a computerized pharmacy system that provides for immediate retrieval of previously dispensed drugs at the time the prescription is presented.
Serve as one of the two consultees 247 CMR 9.17(2) names for a responsive measure, without being a compulsory port of call for every finding.
Stand as the recipient whose dispensing or delivery triggers the review, and as the alternative direct consultee 247 CMR 9.17(2) names.

common_traps.text: Treating the screening list as the definition of the duty. In M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A the review may include, but not be limited to, the named items, so exhausting the list is not the same as conducting the review.
Assuming the review is owed only where the patient collects in person. The statute reaches delivery to a person acting on behalf of such patient, and 247 CMR 9.17(1) reaches a patient's agent.
Assuming interactions with nonprescription or over-the-counter drugs fall outside the review. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A names serious interactions with nonprescription or over-the-counter drugs expressly.

Answering a 247 CMR 9.17(1) question from the statutory list. The regulatory list adds over-utilization or under-utilization, drug-food interaction, any significant change in drug, dose, or directions, and any age related contraindications.

Carrying the reasonable-effort standard across the whole of 247 CMR 9.16(7). It qualifies the content duty only; the immediate-retrieval requirement placed on the computerized pharmacy system is unqualified.
Grading the profile rather than the effort. An incomplete profile is not automatically non-compliant, and a pharmacy that never asked cannot shelter behind the same words.

Reading the four works named in 247 CMR 9.17(3) as an exhaustive list, or accepting a superseded edition of one of them because the work is named. The requirement is current standards, and item (e) is other peer-reviewed medical literature.

Assuming that resolving the clinical issue discharges the documentation duty. 247 CMR 9.17(2) requires a pharmacist to document any measures taken in response to a drug utilization review, whatever the outcome.

Offering a logged alert in the dispensing system as the record of the measure taken. The alert is material the DUR may review under 247 CMR 9.17(1); the record required by 247 CMR 9.17(2) is of what the pharmacist did in response.

Reading a consultation named in 247 CMR 9.17(2) as compulsory. Consultation with the prescribing practitioner or direct consultation with the patient or patient's agent are examples of an appropriate measure, not a required sequence.

Applying the inpatient carve-out in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A to a whole pharmacy, or remembering it as a hospital-only carve-out. It runs on the drug dispensed to an inpatient at a hospital or nursing home.
